writing.tone: Peer-to-peer operator tone: confident, transactional, slightly blunt. Leads with proof of real buying behaviour ('I just bought your book', 'I just booked a call with Francesco') to earn the right to critique, then critiques without apology. Compliments are brief and instrumental ('you do a great job listing delvierables', 'you're doing a lot of things right') and exist only to set up the problem. No small talk, no flattery beyond one clause, no rapport-building questions.
writing.vocabulary: Direct-response and paid-media operator vocabulary. Recurring nouns: conversions, booking rate, show up rate, opt in rate, application rate, closing rate, cost per call, cost per live call, cost per sign up, CAC, ROAS, ad spend, front end conversion rates, throughput, bottlenecks, low hanging fruits, friction, drop off, incongruency. Named tools as proof of specificity: Vidalytics, Vturb, GHL, Typeform, Zapier, UseProof, Microsoft Clarity. Named tactics: FAQ, fast action bonuses, attendance bonuses, urgency/scarcity, social proof below the fold, pre-call podcast / podcast VSL, sunken cost fallacy, forced consumption timer, double opt in. Verbs of damage are visceral: stunting, draining, burning, wrecking, tanking, capping, spiking. Casual asides sit next to jargon ('brain dead', 'guru', '27 bucks', 'left right and center'). Frequent typos left in ('vidoe', 'transfrom', 'abandondning', 'delvierables', 'lifitng', 'situtiation') â€” the writing is fast and unproofread.
writing.sentence_style: Short declaratives for the diagnosis, then one longer causal sentence carrying the 'if you do X, then Y happens because Z' logic. Heavy use of 'if/when youâ€¦ you'llâ€¦' conditionals. Frequent colloquial fragments and one-line punchlines ('Less friction = more throughput.', 'You know these better than I do.', 'Again sounds simple, butâ€¦'). Parentheticals used for credential drops and definitions ('(I work with offer owners increase their front end conversion ratesâ€¦)', '(it's a sales asset disguised as a pocast which instantly boosts consumption)'). Ellipses used to create momentum in the newer template ('Just bought the Daily Profits system...'). Quoted prospect-voice dialogue inserted as evidence: '"how much does it cost?" or "do I have time for this?"'. Numbers used freely as ranges ('3-5%', '5-10%', '10-15%', '4-5%', 'past 85%').
writing.pacing: One idea per short paragraph, near-constant line breaks, almost no paragraph over three sentences. Fast opener (1-2 lines), then observation one, then observation two, each expanded for 2-5 short paragraphs, then a fixed close. Two observations only, always â€” remaining problems are withheld as a count. Total length is moderate; the pre-call podcast section is the one place he allows an extended multi-part explanation with 'Firstâ€¦ Secondâ€¦ Thirdâ€¦'.
writing.greeting_style: Two patterns. Older: 'Hey [First],' or 'Hello Tim,' â€” often with the first sentence run onto the same line as the greeting ('Hey Lloyd, I just bought your book and noticed a problem with your page'). Newer: bare first name plus comma on its own line ('Brian,' 'Rob,' 'Joe,' 'Josiah,'). Always first name only, never 'Hi', never a title, never 'Hope you're well'.
writing.cta_style: Low-friction, no-calendar, no-question-mark CTA. Fixed formula: count the remaining problems ('There's another 5 low hanging fruits I spotted stunting your conversions and draining your returns on ad spend'), offer the same deliverable ('I'm happy to break it down even further in a short loom audit' / 'i can break everything down in detail with a video if you want'), then price-anchor with named clients ('People like Alex Neilan, Dior Ray, and Gav Kwok paid me $750 for a similar audit but I'm happy to shoot it over to you for free.'). Never asks for a meeting, never proposes times, never asks 'are you open toâ€¦'. The ask is permission to send a free video, framed as a gift with a price tag on it.
writing.sign_off_style: Older emails: 'Best,' then 'Vlad'. Newer emails: lowercase 'let me know,' then '-Vlad'. No company name, no title, no links, no signature block.

avoided_phrases: No 'Hope you're well' / 'Hope this finds you well'
No calendar-link or 'does Tuesday at 3 work?' asks
No 'I'd love to' / 'excited to' enthusiasm language
No 'let me know if you have any questions'
No formal sign-offs ('Kind regards', 'Sincerely'), no job titles or company boilerplate
No apologising for the critique ('sorry to be blunt', 'no offence')
No case-study numbers or client results beyond the $750 price anchor
No emojis, no exclamation marks in the body

issues_noticed: Missing FAQ at the bottom of the page â€” his single most repeated observation, applied to VSL pages, webinar opt-in pages, low-ticket sales pages and call confirmation pages

Absent urgency/scarcity: no reason to buy now, static urgency copy instead of a live countdown timer ('Our Next Workshop Is In Less Than 2 Days' â†’ real timer), no custom-coded expiry line above the checkout form
Social proof placed below the fold or missing entirely â€” testimonials that should sit directly under the video or under the order form
Application/opt-in form structure: contact info asked first instead of last, low start rate and completion rate, no sunken-cost sequencing
Double opt-in and duplicated data entry between opt-in page and application form (fixable by passing fields through in GHL)
Video mechanics: forced consumption timer contradicting visible video length/play controls, allowing skipping past the pitch
Message-to-page incongruency: ad promise or product name doesn't match the page ('Heikin-Ashi System' vs 'Daily Profits System')
Button colour / contrast against page theme suppressing clickthrough to the application
Copy that sells logically but is emotionally flat â€” outcomes stated as mechanics, not identity outcomes ('being introduced as "the author" on podcasts')
Page order/sequencing â€” leading with mechanism instead of testimonials placed right under the application form
No 'what this is not' section, so the offer isn't differentiated from scam-adjacent competitors
Bonuses framed as sign-up rewards rather than attendance bonuses (show-up rate lever)
No FOMO/live sign-up notifications on the opt-in page (UseProof)

diagnostic.framing: Everything is framed as a leak in a paid-traffic machine, not as taste or design preference. The frame is always 'this specific missing element is costing you a measurable rate, which is costing you ad dollars'. Problems are almost always framed as ABSENCE ('the lack ofâ€¦', 'you're notâ€¦', 'there's noâ€¦', 'doesn'tâ€¦') or as MISSED OPPORTUNITY, rather than as something they did badly â€” so the critique lands on a gap, not on their competence. He also frames himself as a real customer who walked the funnel ('I just signed up', 'Just got to the end of your application'), which makes the critique observational rather than speculative. Recurring market frame: consumers are sceptical and scammed ('trust recession', 'sales resistance', 'just another "guru"'), so trust-building elements are non-optional.

diagnostic.issue_to_impact: Every observation is bolted to a metric in the same sentence or the one after, using a small set of connective grammar: 'which is stunting you from hitting a 4-5% conversion rate', 'which is limiting your show up rate', 'which is draining your ad budget', 'that not only stunts your show rate but also caps your closing rate', 'effectively decreasing your cost per sign up'. The chain is usually three links: missing element â†’ prospect behaviour (they leave, they skip, they go searching for answers elsewhere, they associate you with the gurus) â†’ metric and money (booking rate, CPA, ROAS, CAC). He frequently quantifies the lift with a range ('bump the clickthrough rate to the application page by 3-5%', 'increase event show up rates by 5-10%') and occasionally scales it into dollars ('an additional 5 figures+ at your scale'). Numbers are stated as expected ranges from experience, never sourced.
diagnostic.observation_to_offer: Each observation is a self-contained mini-consult: he names the gap, explains the buyer psychology behind it, then hands over the actual fix â€” including the tool and sometimes the literal copy ('add a text above the checkout form that's custom coded to say "Your 100% OFF Discount Expires [TOMORROW's DATE]"') or a scripted example question in the prospect's own market ('Now Andrew, I speak with restuarant owners everyday who are concerned they don't have enough timeâ€¦'). He gives away enough that the fix is implementable without him, then converts the remainder into the ask: a fixed count of unnamed problems ('There's another 5 low hanging fruits', 'There's 7 bottlenecksâ€¦ I'll list the first 2 and you can decide if they apply'), a free deliverable (short loom audit / video), and a price anchor via named clients at $750. The offer is never for a call â€” it's for the audit.
diagnostic.observation_structure: Slot 1 â€” PROOF OF ENTRY (subject line + first line): a past-tense action he actually took, verbatim, naming the product or the rep. Openers used: 'I just booked a call with Francesco from your team.' / 'I just bought your Digital Creator bundle and noticed a problem with your page' / 'Just watche the webinar and applied for ez direct sales...'. Slot 2 â€” VERDICT + STAKE (newer template only): 'And I noticed you're doing a lot of things right, but I found something pretty critical that could be wrecking your booking rate on the page...' Slot 3 â€” CREDENTIAL PARENTHETICAL (newer template only): '(I work with offer owners increase their front end conversion rates and decrease their cost per call, so I have a good idea of what converts best)'. Slot 4 â€” SCOPE COUNT (sometimes): 'There's 7 bottlenecks that are pulling back your sign up rates. I'll list the first 2 and you can decide if they apply.' Slot 5 â€” OBSERVATION ONE, opened with 'The first thing I noticed is' followed by an absence ('the lack ofâ€¦' / 'you're notâ€¦' / 'you don'tâ€¦') plus a metric clause ('which is limiting your show up rate'). Slot 6 â€” WHY IT HAPPENS: buyer psychology in 1-3 short paragraphs, often with quoted prospect thoughts ('"how much does it cost?" or "do I have time for this?"') or a market condition ('Consumers today have the highest levels of sales resistance than ever before'). Slot 7 â€” THE FIX: 'a simple tweak would be toâ€¦' / 'There's a simple fix for this by integrating Typeform with Zapier and GHLâ€¦' / 'I would replace this withâ€¦' â€” named tool, placement, sometimes literal copy. Slot 8 â€” PAYOFF: 'you'll see your sign up rate and attendance rate jump up' / 'effectively decreasing your cost per sign up', often with a percentage range. Slot 9 â€” OBSERVATION TWO, opened with 'The second thing I noticed is' / 'The second thing I spotted' / 'The second problem I saw is' / 'A second conversion breaker is', then Slots 6-8 repeated. Slot 10 â€” WITHHELD REMAINDER + OFFER: 'There's another 5 low hanging fruits I spotted stunting your conversions and draining your returns on ad spend, I'm happy to break it down even further in a short loom audit.' Slot 11 â€” PRICE ANCHOR: 'People like Alex Neilan, Dior Ray, and Gav Kwok paid me $750 for a similar audit but I'm happy to shoot it over to you for free.' Slot 12 â€” SIGN OFF: 'Best, Vlad' or 'let me know, -Vlad'.
diagnostic.directness: Very blunt at the level of assertion â€” he states the problem as fact, in the second person, with violent verbs: 'you're losing conversions by not including an FAQ', 'which is draining your ad budget', 'something pretty critical that is wrecking your show up rate', 'This is confusing and people drop off'. He softens with a fixed set of devices that never retract the claim: (1) absence framing so the fault is a gap, not a failure â€” 'the lack ofâ€¦', 'a missed opportunity'; (2) a single specific compliment before the hit â€” 'you're doing a lot of things right, butâ€¦', 'I want to be clear, you do a great job listing delvierables butâ€¦', 'You clearly outline what the book isâ€¦ but'; (3) pre-empting dismissal of small fixes â€” 'The first thing I noticed might sound simple but it's stunting your application rate', 'Again sounds simple, butâ€¦', 'These 2 tweaks might sound simple butâ€¦'; (4) handing them authority over their own market â€” 'You know these better than I do', 'which I'm sure you know', 'You can find the specific questionsâ€¦ from your sales call objections'; (5) giving them the veto â€” 'you can decide if they apply'; (6) earned-standing parentheticals instead of self-praise â€” '(so I have a good idea of what converts best)'; (7) hedged verbs when he can't verify â€” 'could be wrecking', 'which I believe is sitting below', 'My guess isâ€¦', 'to a degree'. He never apologises and never softens the money consequence.
diagnostic.downstream_reasoning: He routinely comments on stages he could only partly see â€” confirmation pages, pre-call texts and emails, sales-call dynamics, closing rate â€” and keeps it from reading as guesswork with three grammars. (1) ABSENCE, stated as fact about something checkable: 'your application form doesn't transfrom in any of the answers into personalized call confirmation text messages', 'the lack of an FAQ section on your page. This one's critical for call confirmations pages like yours', 'The second problem I saw is the lack of pre-call consumption material.' Because he actually booked the call, he can assert what was missing rather than what is wrong. (2) OPPORTUNITY, which asserts a gap without claiming to know their internals: 'The second thing I noticed is a missed opportunity on your Call Confirmation Page to pre-handle objections, that not only stunts your show rate but also caps your closing rate.' (3) RECOMMENDATION plus explicitly-flagged inference, used whenever he's reasoning about the call itself or their internal data: 'My guess is you hear Sonny complain about people showing up to the call with no trust or idea on what it is about.', 'I assume that you want to stay FTC compliant at your scale', 'which I believe is sitting below a 15% start rate and 50% completion rate', 'their objectons will be pre-handled (to a degree)'. He also transfers authority for the unseen facts to them â€” 'All you need is your top 6-8 objections which I'm sure you know', 'You can find the specific questions that need to be included from your sales call objections', 'You know these better than I do' â€” so the unverifiable part is their knowledge, not his claim. Forward-looking claims are always conditional, never predictive of their current numbers: 'When you add an FAQ you can ease whatever uncertainty they still haveâ€¦', 'If they feel like you actually care compared to every other guru out there, they will watch the precall assets and show up.', 'This will do a few things at once. Firstâ€¦ Secondâ€¦ Thirdâ€¦'. He also cites a verification method the prospect can run themselves, which converts a guess into a testable claim: 'If you install microsoft clarity to record use sessions on the VSL and Webinar page, you'll notice a large chunk of them will scroll around the page during the first 30-60 seconds.'

notes: He always buys, opts in, applies or books before writing. The proof-of-entry line is the entire permission structure of the email and it names a specific artefact â€” the rep ('Francesco', 'Daniel', 'Sonny'), the product ('Digital Creator bundle', 'Bookkeeping Challenge', 'Daily Profits system'), or the stage reached ('Just got to the end of your application').

Subject lines are lowercase, 3-7 words, and simply restate the action taken: 'booked a call with Francesco', 'bought your book and noticed a problem', 'signed up for your bnb workshop'. Never a question, never a benefit claim, never a company name.
Exactly two observations per email, every time, then a withheld count of 5 (occasionally 3, or '7 bottlenecksâ€¦ I'll list the first 2'). The withheld remainder is the mechanism of the CTA.
The offer is always a free video audit price-anchored at $750 with the same 2-3 named clients (Alex Neilan, Dior Ray, Gav Kwok). Framing varies: 'clients like', 'People like', 'Founders like'.

Two visible template generations. Older: 'Hey [Name],' + 'I just [action] and noticed a problemâ€¦' + 'Best, Vlad'. Newer: bare '[Name],' + 'Just [action]...' + 'And I noticed you're doing a lot of things right, but I found something pretty critical thatâ€¦' + parenthetical credential + 'i can break everything down in detail with a video if you want' + 'let me know, -Vlad'. The newer version adds the compliment-then-critique pivot and the self-positioning line.

The credential parenthetical is rewritten to match the prospect's funnel type: 'I work with offer owners increase their show up rate past 85% and decrease their cost per live call' for a confirmation-page email, 'I help low ticket offer owners increase low ticket conversion rates past 5% on cold traffic' for a $27 offer.

Examples are always localised to the prospect's ICP â€” 'parents', 'restuarant owners', 'teachers', 'veterans', 'aspiring coaches', 'guys', 'traders' â€” and the podcast script is rewritten with the prospect's own first name and market.
Heavy template reuse across recipients: the FAQ paragraph, the pre-call podcast block and the CTA are near-verbatim across many emails, with only the funnel type, metric and ICP swapped.

Typos, missing words and broken sentences are left in and appear in the shipped copy ('vidoe', 'transfrom', 'delvierables', 'framed as long as it's framed as', 'you'll also .', 'Just watche the webinar', 'The a solution:'). The writing is not proofread.

Numbered lists appear only when a single observation has multiple discrete solutions ('The 2 solutions are: 1. Adding an FAQ 2. Add a pre-call podcast') or as an inline First/Second/Third enumeration of downstream effects. He does not bullet the whole email.
Emphasis is done with capitals on single words ('BUY NOW', 'NOW'), quoted copy, and quoted prospect dialogue â€” never bold, italics or exclamation marks.
Recurring psychological levers he names explicitly: sunken cost fallacy, FOMO, trust recession, sales resistance, meeting them half way, friction/throughput, 'brain dead' scroll behaviour.
